title: Fall Cannabis Edibles: How to Host a Bake-Off at Home
h1: A Fall Edible Bake-Off: Infusing, Dosing and Seasonal Baking
metaDescription: Bake fall cannabis edibles at home: how to decarb, infuse butter or oil, estimate THC per serving, run a friendly bake-off and label and store what you make.
excerpt: Pumpkin, apple and warm spice suit infused baking. Here's how to decarb, infuse and do the dosing math before you bake, then host a friendly bake-off and label every piece.
keyTakeaways: Do the dosing math before you choose a recipe: grams of flower times its THC percentage gives the most THC a batch could hold.
Decarb first. In a lab study, nearly all the THCA converted within about 30 minutes at 230°F; home ovens are less exact.
Think of every estimate as a ceiling, since some THC is lost in the oven and some stays in the plant material you strain out.
Label every piece with its estimated THC, skip candy-like shapes and lock leftovers away from kids and pets.
Keep the bake-off a free, private gathering of adults 21 and older; homemade edibles can't be sold in Michigan.
body:
Fall cannabis edibles make the most of the season's best baking flavors. Pumpkin, apple, brown sugar and warm spice help balance the herbal taste of infused butter, and pan bars and quick breads cut into even pieces. An edible bake-off with friends at home is a fun way to try them, as long as the dosing math comes before the mixing bowl. This guide walks adults 21 and older through decarbing, infusing, estimating THC per serving, a fall recipe lineup, two seasonal sips and how to host, store and share it all responsibly.

## Why fall flavors suit infused baking

Infused butter and oil carry a grassy, herbal flavor. Bold fall flavors such as cinnamon, nutmeg, ginger, clove, molasses and maple stand up to it instead of letting it take over. Dense bakes like bars, blondies and quick breads also hold infused fat well, which makes cannabis baking more forgiving.

Even pieces matter more than you might think. When a pan is cut into a neat grid, each square holds roughly the same share of THC. Free-form cookies and drop scones are harder to keep consistent.

There's a flip side: a delicious edible is easy to overeat. That's one more reason to keep doses low, label everything and put the extras away.

## Decarboxylation: what it is and how to decarb weed at home

Raw cannabis contains mostly THCA, an acid form that has to be heated before it delivers the effects people associate with THC. That heating step is called decarboxylation, or decarbing, and a low-heat infusion may not finish it. In a University of Mississippi lab study of cannabis extract, an hour at temperatures under 212°F (100°C) still left the conversion unfinished. Held at 230°F (110°C), nearly all of the THCA converted within about half an hour.

A simple home method:

1. Heat your oven to about 240°F. An inexpensive oven thermometer helps, since many ovens run hot or cold.
2. Break the flower into small pieces, not powder, and spread it on a parchment-lined baking sheet.
3. Bake for 30 to 45 minutes, gently shaking the tray halfway through, until the flower looks dry and lightly toasted.
4. Let it cool before you infuse it.

Expect a strong smell, so open a window or run the vent fan. Our [decarboxylation guide](/blog/cannabis-decarboxylation/) compares oven, jar and water-bath methods in more detail.

## Dosing math: estimating THC per serving

Homemade edibles dosage comes down to simple math, and it belongs before the recipe:

**Grams of flower × THC percentage × 1,000 = the most THC, in milligrams, the batch could contain.**

| Starting flower | Most THC possible | Spread over 24 squares | Spread over 48 squares |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 g at 15% THC | 150 mg | About 6 mg each | About 3 mg each |
| 2 g at 18% THC | 360 mg | About 15 mg each | About 7.5 mg each |
| 3.5 g at 20% THC | 700 mg | About 29 mg each | About 15 mg each |

If you make infused butter, apply the same thinking to the portion you use. When a cup of butter holds at most 150 mg and the recipe calls for half a cup, the pan holds at most 75 mg.

These numbers are ceilings, not promises. Some THC is lost in the oven: about 8% of the total in that controlled lab study, and a home oven is far less controlled. More stays behind in the plant material you strain out, and uneven mixing makes some pieces stronger than others. For comparison, a store-bought adult-use edible in Michigan holds no more than 10 mg of THC per serving. If your math lands well above that, cut smaller pieces or use less flower.

Start with one small piece and wait. The CDC warns that an edible's effects may not show up for as long as two hours, and Health Canada puts full effects at up to 4 hours. Our [THC dosage guide](/blog/thc-dosage-guide/) covers serving sizes in more depth.

## Infusion bases: butter, oil and tinctures

**Butter.** Cannabutter for baking is the classic base for brownies, bars and cookies. Infuse decarbed flower in butter with a little water over very low heat for a few hours, warm enough to steam but never hot enough to bubble, then strain. Our [cannabutter recipe](/blog/canna-butter-recipe/) walks through each step.

**Oil.** Coconut oil or a neutral oil works the same way and suits recipes that call for oil, such as some cakes and quick breads. It's also a dairy-free option.

**Tinctures.** A store-bought tincture takes much of the guesswork out of dosing, because its label lists its THC content. It's handiest in things you don't bake, such as a glaze, frosting or drink: stir in a measured amount and divide by the number of servings.

A few habits protect both taste and strength:

- **Keep the heat low.** Scorched butter tastes bitter, and too much heat for too long can cost you THC.
- **Strain well.** Leftover plant bits add a grassy flavor.
- **Mix thoroughly.** Stir infused fat evenly through the batter so the pieces come out consistent.
- **Store it apart.** Keep infused butter or oil labeled, sealed and in the fridge, away from your everyday butter.

## Fall cannabis edibles: a recipe lineup

Here's a lineup that covers the season, from pumpkin cannabis recipes to a spread for apple slices:

| Bake | Base | Why it suits a bake-off | Dosing tip |
|---|---|---|---|
| Frosted pumpkin bars | Cannabutter | Bakes in a pan and cuts into a neat grid | Infuse the bars or the frosting, not both |
| Brownies | Cannabutter | A classic that slices evenly | Cut the grid before serving |
| Dump cake | Butter over fruit and cake mix | Easy for first-time bakers | Spread the infused butter evenly; scoop equal portions |
| No-bake oatmeal cookies | Cannabutter | No oven needed after the decarb | Use a cookie scoop for even sizes |
| Chocolate swirl banana bread | Butter or oil | Slices are easy to count | Mark the loaf so slices stay even |
| Infused almond butter | Oil or butter blended in | A spread for apples and crackers | Measure servings by the teaspoon |

Try the [pumpkin bars](/blog/infused-pumpkin-bars/) or the [brownies](/blog/pot-brownies-recipe/) first, and find the rest in our [cannabis recipes collection](/blog/recipes/).

## Fall sips: an infused spiced latte and apple cider

Warm drinks round out a bake-off, and they're easy to dose one mug at a time.

**Spiced latte.** Warm milk or oat milk with maple syrup and a pinch of pumpkin pie spice, froth it and pour it over strong coffee or espresso. For an infused mug, stir in one measured tincture dose at the end. The recipe card below has the details.

**Mulled apple cider.** Warm apple cider with a cinnamon stick, a few cloves and a strip of orange peel until it steams. Ladle it into mugs, then add a measured tincture dose to each infused mug. Never infuse the whole pot, since that turns every cup into a guess.

For both drinks, make plenty of non-infused mugs, label the infused ones and keep everything alcohol-free. The CDC says using alcohol and cannabis at the same time is likely to cause more impairment than either one alone.

## Running a friendly bake-off at home

A bake-off is a great excuse to gather, and a few house guidelines keep it that way.

- **Keep it private, adult and free.** Invite adults 21 and older to a private home. Michigan lets adults give cannabis to other adults 21 and older only when nothing is received in return and the gift isn't advertised to the public, so skip entry fees, ticket sales and public invitations. Homemade edibles can't be sold, either: in Michigan, only licensed marijuana businesses may sell marijuana products.
- **Judge the twins.** Ask each baker to bring two versions: a non-infused batch for judging and a labeled infused batch for later. Tasting six infused entries in one afternoon would stack doses fast, so keep the judging THC-free.
- **Set a house cap.** Agree on a top THC amount per piece before anyone bakes, such as 5 mg, and have each baker show their math on a card.
- **Portion and label.** Cut bite-size pieces, use one plate per entry and add a card with the baker's name, the estimated THC per piece and the words "contains THC."
- **Skip kid-appealing looks.** No gummy bears, animal shapes, cartoon decorations or anything that looks like candy. Michigan bars licensed edibles shaped like people, animals or fruit, and that's a smart standard for home bakers too.
- **Plan the evening.** Set out the infused bakes early, keep regular food and water out and line up rides home. Nobody who has consumed cannabis should drive.

## Storing, labeling and sharing responsibly

When the judging is done, the job is to keep everything clearly marked and out of the wrong hands.

- **Label every container.** Write "contains THC," the estimated THC per piece and the date you made it.
- **Store it like food, and then some.** Follow normal storage for the recipe: refrigerate anything with cream cheese or other perishables, and freeze extras, sealed airtight, for longer keeping. Keep everything cool, dark and sealed, since THC can break down with light and air.
- **Lock it up.** Store edibles where children and pets can't get to them, ideally in a locked box, and never mixed in with regular desserts.
- **Share carefully.** Give edibles only to adults 21 and older who know what they're getting, and never in exchange for anything.
- **Stay in Michigan.** Don't travel across state lines with cannabis.

If you'd rather skip the math, store-bought edibles and tinctures come in labeled, pre-measured servings, and our budtenders can help you compare options. 21+ only. Please consume responsibly.

faq.q: How do I figure out how strong my homemade edibles are?
faq.a: Multiply the grams of flower by its THC percentage, then by 1,000. That gives the most THC, in milligrams, the batch could hold. Divide by the number of pieces for a per-piece ceiling. Real amounts run lower and vary from piece to piece, so start with one small piece and wait at least 2 hours before having more.

faq.q: Do I need to decarb before making cannabutter?
faq.a: Yes, if you want THC's usual effects. Raw flower holds mostly THCA, and gentle infusion heat may not finish converting it: in a lab study of cannabis extract, an hour below 212°F (100°C) still left the job incomplete. Decarb broken-up flower in a low oven first, let it cool and then infuse it into your butter.

faq.q: How long do homemade edibles keep?
faq.a: About as long as the same recipe would without cannabis. Refrigerate anything perishable, such as cream cheese frosting, and freeze extras in airtight containers if you want them to last longer. Keep them cool, dark and sealed, label each container with the date and the THC per piece, and store it all out of reach of kids and pets.

faq.q: Can I use a tincture instead of cannabutter?
faq.a: Yes, and it can make dosing easier, since a store-bought tincture's label lists its THC content. It works best in frostings, glazes and drinks: stir in a measured amount and divide by the number of servings. In Michigan, an adult-use tincture dose holds no more than 10 mg of THC. Expect a little flavor from the tincture itself.

ingredients: 1/2 cup strong brewed coffee or 2 shots espresso
1/4 teaspoon pumpkin pie spice, plus a pinch for the top
A measured dose of THC tincture, kept small
steps: Warm the milk, maple syrup and spice in a small pot on medium-low heat, whisking, until it steams. Don't let it boil.
Froth the milk with a whisk or a handheld frother until foamy.
Pour the coffee into a mug and top it with the spiced milk.
Off the heat, stir in one measured tincture dose. Make every other mug without it.
Finish with whipped cream and a pinch of spice, and tag the infused mug so nobody mixes it up.
recipe.dosingNote: THC per mug = the THC in the amount of tincture you add. If a label says a 1 mL dose holds 10 mg, a quarter of that dose adds about 2.5 mg. Michigan labels note that actual values may vary by 10%, and homemade tinctures vary much more, since their strength depends on the flower's potency and on what's lost during decarbing and infusing. Consider the number an estimate. Start with a small dose, wait at least 2 hours before having more, label every infused mug and keep it away from children and pets.

review.summary: 21 claims checked: 19 ok, 2 fixed (0 wrong, 0 unsupported, 2 overstated); 1 ok claim also got a precision edit (the lab study used cannabis extract).

claims.claim: Raw cannabis contains mostly THCA, which must be heated (decarboxylated) to give THC's usual effects (body, FAQ 1)
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5549281/ (Wang 2016, full text via Europe PMC): neutral cannabinoids "do not occur at significant concentrations in the plants"; the acids "can be decarboxylated when exposed to light or heat via smoking, baking, or refluxing"

claims.claim: "a warm infusion alone won't finish it" / "gentle infusion heat won't finish converting it" (body, FAQ 1)
claims.fix: now "a low-heat infusion may not finish it" and "may not finish converting it": the study only shows incomplete conversion within 60 minutes below 100°C; its own first-order rate constant at 95°C (0.66 x 10^-3 per second) implies near-complete conversion over a multi-hour infusion at that temperature, while at 80°C (0.18 x 10^-3) much would remain
claims.source: PMC5549281: "At temperatures lower than 100°C, the reaction did not reach completion within 60 min"; Table 2 rate constants for THCA-A in extracts: 0.18 (80°C), 0.66 (95°C), 1.83 (110°C) x 10^-3 sec^-1

claims.claim: University of Mississippi lab study: under 212°F (100°C) an hour left conversion unfinished; at 230°F (110°C) nearly all THCA converted within about 30 minutes (body, takeaway 1, FAQ 1)
claims.fix: precision edit: body and FAQ now say "lab study of cannabis extract" (dried extracts in a vacuum oven, not flower)
claims.source: PMC5549281: authors at the National Center for Natural Products Research, University of Mississippi; "the concentration of THCA-A approached zero in 30, 9, and 6 min at 110°C, 130°C, and 145°C"; "C. sativa extracts were used" in "a vacuum oven"

claims.claim: Home method: about 240°F for 30 to 45 minutes, broken-up flower on a parchment-lined tray, cool before infusing
claims.source: presented as a home method, consistent with PMC5549281 (THCA near zero after about 30 minutes at 110°C/230°F); the copy notes home ovens run hot or cold

claims.claim: Grams x THC percentage x 1,000 = the most THC in mg; table values (150 mg: about 6 or 3 mg per square; 360 mg: about 15 or 7.5; 700 mg: about 29 or 15); half a cup of a 150 mg cup of butter = at most 75 mg (body, takeaway 0, FAQ 0)
Estimates are ceilings: about 8% was lost in the controlled lab study, more stays in strained plant material, and uneven mixing varies pieces (body, takeaway 2)
claims.source: PMC5549281 Table 1: relative loss in total molar concentration upon completion of THCA-A decarboxylation "7.94"%; strained-material and mixing losses stated qualitatively

claims.claim: A store-bought adult-use edible in Michigan holds no more than 10 mg THC per serving
claims.source: facts/law-facts.json mi-thc-limits (CRA technical bulletin, April 24, 2025): "adult-use 10 mg/dose, 200 mg/container"

claims.claim: The CDC warns edible effects may take up to two hours to show; Health Canada puts full effects at up to 4 hours (body, FAQ 0, dosing note)

claims.claim: A store-bought tincture's "label lists the THC per serving" (body, FAQ 3)
claims.fix: now "its label lists its THC content": the Michigan label rule requires THC concentration; a per-serving figure is not a documented requirement (same correction as the batch's charcuterie article)

review.notes: Independent fact-check: Wang 2016 full text read through Europe PMC (Results, Table 1 losses, Table 2 rate constants); CDC FAQ and Health Canada page reopened with WebFetch; Michigan limits, labels, edible shapes, gifting and sale rules matched to facts/law-facts.json. All seven sources exist, are https and support the text. Recipe card matches contract section 4 (yield, prepTime, cookTime, ingredients, steps, dosingNote); the dosing note shows the math as an estimate, says start low and wait, and to label and keep away from children and pets. H1 "Baking Seasonal Treats" became "Seasonal Baking": docs/VOICE.md lists "treat" among words High Society never uses, and the gate flagged it. Recipe step 1 reworded ("small saucepan over medium-low" to "small pot on medium-low") after the overlap check began grading recipe cards and flagged a 6-word stock phrase. Low-risk article: no brands, no High Society event or contest, kid-appealing shapes ruled out. Writer's notes: Low-risk seasonal baking guide. No precise potency promises (math shown as a ceiling with named losses); infusion loss given qualitatively (no reliable home-infusion figure found in PubMed); no branded edibles; no suggestion that High Society runs a contest or event; kid-appealing shapes ruled out. Body links capped at 6 (decarb, dosage, cannabutter, pumpkin bars, brownies, the Recipes category for the rest of the lineup); dump cake, banana bread and cider recipes in related. The latte has no planned recipe page, so it carries the recipe card.
